[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance defines how **application-layer authorization** (RBAC/ABAC and related access invariants that span nodes) is authored as a **design-first `cross-cutting` seam in OPA/Rego policy-as-code**, with a strict **design-vs-implementer ownership split** so that no implementer authors the policy that gates its own output. It is the cross-cutting class of the design-first seam model ([PTN-APP-API-040](../../../../patterns/application/api-microservices/PTN-APP-API-040-design-first-seam-contract-pattern.md)) and the security-domain companion to the invariant standard ([STD-GOV-QA-002](../../../../standards/governance/quality/STD-GOV-QA-002-invariant-verification-standard.md)).
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- **Closes the cross-cutting seam gap** — authorization is an edge that spans nodes; like other edges it is easily left unowned (a route ships with no policy decision). Making it a design-first Rego seam gives it an owner and a gate.
- **Prevents fox-guarding-henhouse** — the party whose output the policy constrains does not author the policy; this is essential when AI agents implement endpoints that a policy must gate.
- **Audit-ready authorization** — a Rego policy with `opa test` in CI is defensible HIPAA/NIST evidence, unlike authorization logic scattered in application code.
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Security & solution architects** — author the authorization decision and Rego rules (the design side).
- **Platform/deployer engineers and agents** — wire enforcement (OPA sidecar/gateway/middleware).
- **Developers & AI coding agents** — implement gated endpoints against, not around, the policy.
page_texts.7:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#scope-and-applicability]

### Scope and Applicability

Applies to application-layer authorization for any capability with access-control obligations. Covers authoring authz as a Rego cross-cutting seam, the ownership split, and verification. It does **not** cover: authentication/identity mechanisms (→ IAM guidance, OpenAPI `securitySchemes`); infrastructure policy-as-code for Terraform/K8s admission (→ PTN-INFRA-GOV-002); the error-envelope shape (→ the sync-api OpenAPI RFC 7807 responses); or observability.
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#authorization-is-a-cross-cutting-seam-not-node-behavior]

### Authorization is a cross-cutting seam, not node behavior

An authorization rule is not the behavior of any single node — it is an invariant that spans every node in its scope ("no route in `claims` serves data without an allow decision"). Under behavior-only decomposition it has no scenario, no work item, and no gate, so it is implemented ad hoc inside each handler (or forgotten in one). Treating it as a **cross-cutting seam** authored once in Rego makes it a single owned, verifiable artifact that every in-scope node depends on (a T1 prerequisite via the `AUTH-FOUNDATION`).
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#why-oparego]

### Why OPA/Rego

OPA/Rego is CNCF-graduated and already the enterprise engine for policy-as-code (RBAC/authz, IaC/K8s admission, CI gates). Using it for application authz means one recognized policy language a reviewer already knows, decidable and testable with `opa test`, decoupled from application code.
page_texts.11:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#why-the-ownership-split]

### Why the ownership split

Because an authorization rule is a **negative/compliance invariant** ("must never allow X"), the party whose output it constrains must not author it — an agent implementing an endpoint must not also write the policy that decides whether that endpoint may serve data. Authorship is therefore split across decision, wiring, and verification.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#the-three-seam-classes-and-where-authz-sits]

### The three seam classes and where authz sits

Authz is the **`cross-cutting`** class of the seam model (the other classes being `sync-api` → OpenAPI and `event` → AsyncAPI). Its native standard is **OPA/Rego**; the 401/403 response shapes it implies are documented in the relevant `sync-api` OpenAPI operations.
page_texts.14:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#the-ownership-split-normative]

### The ownership split (normative)

| Concern | Owner | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Policy **decision + Rego rules** | human-directed design (`/architect`, logical-arch Phase 6) | The decision and the Rego SHALL be authored by design, never by the implementer/agent whose output the policy gates. |
| Enforcement **wiring** (OPA sidecar / gateway / middleware / the `AUTH-FOUNDATION` issue) | platform/deployer (may be agent output) | Mechanical integration of a decided policy MAY be implementer/agent output. |
| **Verification** | independent (`opa test` on the Rego + a no-bypass fitness/property check) | Verification SHALL be independent of the implementer and MUST be CI-invoked. |

The authorization property itself SHALL also be registered as an `INV-*` invariant (STD-GOV-QA-002) — typically an `architecture` (no-bypass reachability) invariant plus, where decisions have value logic, a `property` invariant.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#authoring-the-rego-seam]

### Authoring the Rego seam

- Author policy under `docs/design/seam-contracts/cross-cutting/<scope>.rego` (design-time, before the gated endpoints are dispatched).
- Express decisions as explicit `allow` rules with default-deny; keep rules data-driven (roles/attributes as input) rather than hard-coded per endpoint.
- Document, in the gated `sync-api` OpenAPI operations, the 401/403 responses the policy produces.
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#steps]

### Steps

1. **Identify** the access-control obligations spanning the capability's nodes; state each as a "never allow …" invariant.
2. **Author** (design) the Rego policy for the scope; register the `INV-*` (STD-GOV-QA-002); default-deny.
3. **Declare** the `AUTH-FOUNDATION` as a T1 prerequisite for every in-scope feature (foundation-before-fan-out).
4. **Wire** enforcement (deployer/agent) — sidecar/gateway/middleware calling OPA.
5. **Verify** independently — `opa test` on the Rego + a no-bypass fitness check (the `policy` and `architecture` test types, STD-APP-TEST-001), CI-invoked.
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#verification-checklist]

### Verification checklist

- `opa test` runs in CI and covers allow/deny cases.
- A no-bypass fitness/reachability check proves no in-scope route serves data without a policy decision.
- The authorization `INV-*` is registered and operational.
- The Rego was authored by design, not by the implementer of the gated endpoints.
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#worked-example--claims-read-authorization]

### Worked example — claims read authorization

**Obligation:** "No `claims` route serves PHI without an allow decision; a member may read only their own claims."
**Design:** `/architect` authors `cross-cutting/claims.rego` (default-deny; `allow` when `input.subject.member_id == input.resource.member_id` or role in {adjudicator, auditor}) and registers `INV-CLAIMS-001` (no-bypass, `architecture` tier) + `INV-CLAIMS-003` (own-claims-only, `property` tier).
**Wiring:** deployer wires an OPA sidecar via the `AUTH-FOUNDATION` issue; every claims feature depends on it (T1).
**Verification:** `opa test` (allow/deny cases) + a NetArchTest reachability check that every claims route passes through the decision point — both in CI.
**Outcome:** authorization is one owned, tested seam; the endpoint-implementing agent never authored the policy gating it.
page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/security/implementation/GUID-SEC-IMPL-002-application-authorization-policy-as-code-guidance.md#governance-and-compliance]

## Governance and Compliance

- **Normative weight:** the SHALL/SHOULD statements above carry enforcement weight per the security routing rule.
- **Gate:** `/eap-sdd-health-check` treats the cross-cutting seam as: a `Scope = platform` authz constraint SHALL resolve to a governing Rego policy (else it is the missing-middle for cross-cutting concerns), and Phase 11 verifies runtime enforcement.
- **HIPAA / NIST 800-53 r5:** access-control invariants (AC family) are compliance-critical; authoring them as tested Rego with independent verification provides audit evidence. PHI-access negatives are mandatory invariants (STD-GOV-QA-002).
- **Ownership:** the design-vs-implementer split is mandatory for agentic delivery (an agent must not author its own gate).
